title: The recipe no one asked you to change
hook: Pepsi keeps winning taste tests. Do you change the world's most famous recipe?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: How much cola you sell today

future.label: Loyalty
future.hint: How much your fans love and trust Coke

intro.text: Atlanta, USA, 1984. You run Coca-Cola, the world's best-known drink, made almost the same way for nearly 100 years. Coke still sells more than Pepsi, but for 15 years, Pepsi has been getting closer. Your board wants you to stop losing your lead.

s_challenge.text: Since 1975, Pepsi has run the Pepsi Challenge in shops and markets. People taste two colas without seeing the names, and more people choose Pepsi. Your own team does the same test and gets the same result: people like a sweeter taste.

d1.title: How to keep your lead
d1.setup: There is some good news. Diet Coke, launched in 1982, shows that new drinks can bring in buyers. While making it, your lab also found a sweeter recipe that beat both Pepsi and your old Coke in taste tests.
d1.question: How do you keep your lead?
d1.advisor: Pepsi says our taste is the problem, and our own tests show the same thing.

options.label: Make a new, sweeter Coke in secret. It may win, but the old recipe changes.
options.outcome: You decide taste is the problem. A team works in secret on a sweeter recipe, and in tests with nearly 200,000 people, it beats both Pepsi and the old Coke.
options.why: Remember: sell what it means to them, not just what it is. Taste is only one fact about the drink. Coke was part of people's lives and memories, but your team was getting ready to change the recipe those fans loved.
options.better: Keep the old recipe. Bring in buyers with new drinks and fresh ads, as Diet Coke did, and test new tastes as extra drinks.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you tried to solve a problem about feelings by changing the flavour.

options.label: Keep the recipe and use new drinks and ads. Fans stay happy, but Pepsi keeps gaining.
options.outcome: You keep the recipe and spend your money on new drinks and fresh ads. Pepsi keeps gaining for a while, and your board wants faster results. But fans still get the taste they grew up with, and Diet Coke keeps bringing in new buyers.
options.why: Remember: sell what it means to them, not just what it is. Taste was only one fact about the drink. Your name, your history and your fans' memories mattered more than which drink won a taste test.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you grew your business without changing your main drink.

options.label: Cut prices to give families more Coke for less. Sales may rise, but profit per can falls.
options.outcome: Cheaper Coke brings back some buyers, but then Pepsi cuts its prices too. Now both companies earn less on every can, and Pepsi is still getting closer to Coke.
options.why: Remember: sell what it means to them, not just what it is. Price is also just a number, and Pepsi could match your price in a week. Cutting prices also made fans think Coke was worth less.
options.better: Keep your price. Give people new reasons to buy Coke, like new drinks and fresh ads.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you used lower prices to fight Pepsi, but made Coke seem worth less.

d2.title: The drink that won the taste test

setup.text: The sweeter recipe has won your tests. But the tests only checked taste, not how people would feel if the old Coke was gone. About 10 to 12 in every 100 testers said they were angry about changing it.

Your new drinks are selling, but Pepsi is still close behind. Your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe, though a few people in early tests say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

Cutting prices has left you with low profits and no clear win. Your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe, though a few people in early tests say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

d2.question: What do you do with the new recipe?
d2.advisor: One Coke makes advertising simpler, and the new taste wins the tests. But people have drunk the old one all their lives.

options.label: Sell the new taste as a second Coke. Fans keep the old one, but two Cokes may confuse buyers.
options.outcome: The sweet drink goes into shops beside the old Coke. Pepsi cannot tell a story about angry Coke fans, and your fans still have the drink they love.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. The new taste might give people a better taste when they take a sip. The old Coke kept the feeling people loved, so fans did not lose their favourite drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you gave buyers a new choice without taking away the old one.

options.label: Replace the old Coke everywhere. Buyers get one clear Coke, but fans lose the old taste.

outcome.text: On April 23, 1985, at a big event in New York, you announce the first recipe change in 99 years. The old Coke is taken off the market. Pepsi celebrates by giving its staff a day off and putting ads across whole newspaper pages.
You announce the new recipe and stop selling the old Coke. Pepsi celebrates with newspaper ads, and reporters start asking fans what they think.

options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. A taste test shows which drink tastes better, but not how people feel about a drink they grew up with. Your own research warned you that some fans would be angry.
options.better: Sell the new taste as an extra drink beside the old Coke, and keep selling the old one.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you took away the drink fans loved because a test said they liked a new taste more.

options.label: Replace it in a few cities first. You learn more, but it takes longer, and Pepsi will notice.
options.outcome: In a few test cities, the sweet drink replaces the old Coke. Within weeks, people in those cities send you many angry letters, and newspapers soon report the complaints.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Testing in a few cities seemed careful, but you still took away a drink people loved. The anger in those cities was real.
options.better: Test the new taste without removing the old Coke. Sell both drinks together.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tested the change before doing it everywhere, but you still took away the old Coke.

d3.title: The fans get angry

setup.text: By June, about 1,500 fans call your phone line every day, and the angry letters will reach about 40,000 in all. Fans form protest groups and buy as much old Coke as they can. A survey says only 13 in 100 cola drinkers like the new taste. Liking one sip in a test is different from drinking it every day.
Within weeks, your phones ring all day and the letters keep coming. Fans form protest groups and buy as much old Coke as they can find.

d3.question: Your fans are furious. What do you do?
d3.advisor: If we admit we were wrong, the world will see us fail. But if we continue, how many fans will leave?

options.label: Spend more on ads for the new taste. It may bring buyers, but angry fans may get angrier.
options.outcome: You spend a lot on ads for the new taste. A few people start buying it, but most fans feel you are not listening, and more people join the protests.
options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Ads can tell people about a drink, but they cannot make people stop missing something they loved. Each week you defended the new Coke, fans felt you were not listening.
options.better: Admit the mistake quickly. Bring the old recipe back and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you spent money trying to change your fans' minds instead of listening to them.

options.label: Make the new recipe more like the old one. You keep one Coke, but it takes months.
options.outcome: Your lab works all summer to make the new taste more like the old one. But fans do not want a similar taste. They want the real Coke back, and some leave for Pepsi and never return.
options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Fans did not ask you to improve the new taste. They wanted their old Coke back, and every month spent changing the recipe made them angrier.
options.better: Listen to what fans want. Bring the old recipe back quickly and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept changing the new recipe when fans wanted the old Coke back.

options.label: Bring back the old Coke and say sorry. Fans get it back, but everyone sees you were wrong.

outcome.text: On July 11, 1985, just 79 days after the change, you say sorry and bring back the old recipe, now called Coca-Cola Classic. TV channels stop their regular shows to report the news, and your phone line gets 31,600 calls in two days.
Within weeks of the change, you say sorry and bring back the old recipe. The news spreads quickly, and many happy fans call your company.

options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Saying sorry is hard for a big company, but you acted within weeks and gave fans back what they loved.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you admitted a big mistake quickly and fixed it.

d3alt.title: What the buyers showed you

setup.text: The sweet drink is sold beside the old Coke. Sales show that some people like it, but most still choose the taste they grew up with. Your sales team says having two Cokes is confusing shoppers.

In your test cities, many fans are angry because the old Coke is gone. People there still like the sweet drink in taste tests, but they miss the old one. Your team cannot agree on what to do in the rest of the country.

d3alt.question: What next for the sweet recipe?
d3alt.advisor: Most people who tried the new taste liked it. Doesn't that mean we should go ahead?

options.label: Sell the new taste everywhere and replace the old. Tests were good, but fans may object.

outcome.text: Fans across the country get angry, just as people in your test cities warned you. After a summer of protests, you agree to their demands and bring the old Coke back.
When you remove the old Coke from shops, fans across the country get angry. After a summer of protests, you agree to their demands and bring the old Coke back.

options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. Your buyers showed you that most still wanted the old Coke, but you continued anyway. A test only helps if you use what you learn.
options.better: Make the old Coke your main drink, and sell the sweet taste only as an extra choice.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you ignored what your own tests warned you about.

options.label: Sell it only in towns where it sells best. Sales may grow, but running different Cokes costs more.
options.outcome: The sweet drink sells in a few places, but selling different Cokes in different places costs more and confuses buyers. People are not sure which Coke is the real one.
options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. You had not decided that "some people liked it" was enough to continue. Selling different Cokes in different towns made more work for a small gain.
options.better: Make the old Coke your main drink everywhere, and sell the sweet taste as a clear extra choice.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tried to reduce risk, but made your brand more confusing.

options.label: Keep the old Coke as the main drink and the sweet one as an extra. Fans stay, but growth may be slow.

outcome.text: The old Coke returns to shops in your test cities, with the sweet drink beside it. Fans calm down, and the sweet drink finds a small group of buyers.
Fans keep the Coke they love, and the sweet drink finds a small group of buyers. Slowly, Coke starts to increase its lead over Pepsi again.

options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. Your tests showed that people liked the new taste but loved the old Coke. You used what the tests showed you.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you protected your main drink and gave the new one a chance to prove itself.

text.text: Fans are happy, and Classic sells fast. You keep selling the new drink too, so shops now have two Cokes: Classic and the new, sweeter drink, which still has the name Coca-Cola.
Fans are happy, and the old Coke sells fast again. You keep selling the new drink too, so shops now have two Cokes.

Your lab works all summer, but few fans like the changed recipe, and the protests continue. In the end, you bring the old recipe back, but fans say you listened only when you had no other choice. Now shops have two Cokes.
The ads cost a lot of money but change few minds. Fans protest all summer, and in the end you bring the old recipe back. Now shops have two Cokes.
The old taste is back after a difficult summer, and shops now have two Cokes. Many fans are still angry with you.
In some towns, shoppers find one Coke, but in others they find two. Your sales team wants one clear plan for the whole country.
The old Coke is still the main drink, and the sweet drink has a small group of fans. Pepsi is no longer getting closer to Coke.

d4.title: Money for next year's ads
d4.setup: You have a fixed amount to spend on ads next year, and both drinks need it. The team selling the sweet drink asks for half the money. Your choice will change how people see Coke.
d4.question: How will you divide the ad money?
d4.advisor: Giving each drink half is fair to both teams, and both drinks get a chance to sell more.

options.label: Spend nearly all on old Coke. Fans may buy more, but the sweet drink's team loses support.
options.outcome: You spend your money on the taste your fans chose, and the new drink slowly stops selling. Shoppers know which Coke is the main drink.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Your fans had shown you which Coke gave them the feeling they wanted. You spent your money on that drink instead of one they did not want.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you spent money on what buyers wanted, not what you hoped they would want.

options.label: Give both drinks their own ads. Each gets a chance, but each gets less money.

outcome.text: You keep both drinks and give each its own ads. Classic quickly sells more than the new drink, and within a few months it is again the best-selling regular cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink's share of the market falls to about 3 in 100.
You divide the money and give each drink its own ads. The old Coke sells far more than the new one, and half your ad money goes to a drink few people want.

options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Only one of your two Cokes gave fans the feeling they wanted, but you divided your money and attention between both drinks.
options.better: Spend most of your money on the taste fans chose, and let the new drink slowly stop selling.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you divided your money between a popular drink and one that few people wanted.

options.label: Spend most on sweet Coke. It may attract young buyers, but old Coke gets less support.
options.outcome: You spend money promoting the new drink again. Fans feel you have ignored them for a second time, and many decide to buy Pepsi instead.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Young buyers liked the sweet taste, but your fans had already told you twice which Coke gave them the feeling they wanted.
options.better: Spend more on the drink your fans chose, and let the new one slowly stop selling.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept promoting a drink your buyers had already said they did not want.

text.text: You never took away your fans' favourite drink. New drinks and fresh ads bring in more buyers, and Coke increases its lead over Pepsi without a summer of angry fans.
You listened to what the test showed you. The old Coke stays the main drink, the sweet drink stays a small extra, and Coke increases its lead over Pepsi again.
You made mistakes, but you listened quickly and spent money on the taste your fans loved. Coke ends the year stronger than Pepsi, and its fans know you will listen.

survivor.title: The return of the old Coke

text.text: By the end of 1985, Coca-Cola Classic sells far more than both the new drink and Pepsi. The new drink is later given a new name and stopped in 2002, and Coca-Cola becomes stronger.
The old Coke is back and selling again, but you took a whole summer to listen. Coke stays ahead of Pepsi, and fans remember how long you made them wait.
You spent money on the wrong drink at the end, and some fans leave for Pepsi. Coke is still big and still ahead, but its lead is smaller than before the new drink.
You made some costly choices, but you listened before it was too late. Your fans stay with you, and Coke stays ahead of Pepsi.

collapse.title: The Coke that lost its fans

text.text: You kept promoting the new drink even after fans rejected it twice. Many switch to Pepsi and never return, and the world's best-known drink loses its lead.
By the time you spent money on the taste your fans loved, too many had switched to Pepsi and never returned. The world's best-known drink loses its lead.

fired.title: The board asks you to leave
fired.text: You made three costly decisions. The board no longer trusts you, so it asks someone else to bring the fans back.

realHistory: Coca-Cola was losing ground to Pepsi, which kept winning taste tests where people could not see the names. After tests with nearly 200,000 people, it replaced its 99-year-old recipe with a sweeter one on April 23, 1985. Fans were furious, and calls, letters and protest groups poured in. After 79 days, on July 11, 1985, the company said sorry and brought back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. Within months Classic was again the top regular cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink fell to about 3% of the market and was dropped in 2002.
